Note. We distinguish three time scales: (1) within-burst processes, which unfold over short intervals (e.g., days) during intensive assessment periods; (2) between-burst processes, which occur during gaps between bursts when no testing takes place; and (3) cumulative processes, which reflect short-term learning dynamics (e.g., learning across days) that accrue with repeated exposure across all assessments and persist across bursts. As summarized in Table 1, there are seven key cognitive markers that we can extract with the BDEM: peak (asymptotic) performance (a (i) ), change in asymptotic performance (∆ (i) ), retest gain across study (g C(i) ), learning rate across study (r C(i) ), forgetting between bursts (ϕ (i) ), learning rate within bursts (r W (i) ), and intra-individual variability (τ (i) ). All cognitive markers are captured for each participant as random effects, as the BDEM is implemented in a multilevel Bayesian statistical framework (Gelman et al., 2013). These person-specific parameters are assigned population distributions and can be regressed on person-level predictors in a single-step analysis to quantify sources of individual differences in cognitive performance characteristics while avoiding generated regressor bias that could come from using an estimated variable as an independent variable in a second-step regression (Boehm, Steingroever, & Wagenmakers, 2018; Pagan, 1984).

In a Bayesian framework, every model parameter has to be assigned a prior probability distribution-this corresponds to our knowledge of the likely values of the parameter before taking into account the data. Next, we define the prior distributions and the hyperprior distributions. Hyperpriors are prior distributions assigned to the parameters of another prior distribution. For example, in our model, the population distributions act as priors for an individual's cognitive markers. Because the parameters defining those population distributions (like the group mean) must also be estimated, we must assign them their own priors-these are known as hyperpriors. All our prior distributions will fall into the category of weakly informative (or "non-committal") priors, reflecting that, although we have little knowledge of the likely parameter values, we know their plausible ranges (e.g., learning rates are always positive).

Priors for Person-Level Parameters

The seven cognitive markers in Equation (1) (g C(i) , r C(i) , a (i) , ∆ (i) , ϕ (i) , r W (i) , τ (i) ) are person-specific to capture individual differences in key cognitive functions. We specify a population-level distribution for each marker while respecting its theoretical range. This tutorial introduces a log transformation for positivity in Stan, called the 'logStan' solution.

Parameters are modeled on the log scale and mapped back with an exponential transform, which keeps them on the positive real line. This matches the usual treatment of positivity in regression modeling, and we focus on this solution here.

We will also show an alternative, 'boundedStan', which limits each parameter in its declaration. The sampler then operates on an unconstrained scale internally and transforms the samples back for inference. This does not implement truncated normal inference: the bounds are enforced, but the truncation normalization constant is not included in the likelihood. To keep parameters positive, we use real<lower=0>. This choice allows a more straightforward interpretation of the results. While the 'logStan' parametrization can also be used in PyMC and JAGS, the 'boundedStan' version is limited to Stan.

The gain across the study, g C(i) , is restricted to be positive. This constraint is based on the assumption that repeated practice on a cognitive task does not make people systematically worse at it, and individual differences in the magnitude of the practice gain can be indicative of early risk of cognitive decline. Note that we would keep this definition of the gain parameter even if retest learning were described with a bounded exponential for scores where higher is better; see an illustration of this alternative parametrization in the Discussion. With the 'logStan' approach, we sample the log of person-specific gain parameters (ln(g C(i) )) from a normal distribution: where ln(g C(i) ) is drawn from a normal population distribution with mean β ln(g) C and variance σ 2 ln(g) C , both on the log scale.

With the alternative 'boundedStan' approach, we would achieve the positivity constraint simply by limiting the range of possible values for g C(i) , and then sampling the person-specific gain parameters from a normal distribution: where the suffix b indicates that the distribution is bounded.

For the rest of the person-specific parameters, the population mean is decomposed into a product of person-level predictors and regression coefficients to explain sources of individual differences in these key cognitive markers. The log-transformed learning rates across the study, ln(r C(i) ), are distributed in the 'logStan' model as follows: where X (i) is the covariate vector for person (i), β ln(r) C is the regression coefficient vector and σ ln(r) C is the standard deviation.

In our empirical example, the regression coefficient vector consists of one intercept term and three regression coefficients (i.e., β ln(r) C = β ln(r) C ,0 , β ln(r) C ,1 , β ln(r) C ,2 , β ln(r) C ,3 T ), where a positive regression coefficient would indicate that higher levels of a predictor are associated with greater learning rates. In the 'boundedStan' model, positivity is again enforced through the parameter declarations, followed by a normal sampling statement (i.e., r C(i) ∼ N (X T (i) β r C , σ 2 r C )b(0, +)). The peak performance is distributed as: where β a and σ a denote the regression coefficient vector and standard deviation, respectively.

Although asymptote is positive in this RT example, peak performance need not be positive for all cognitive measures. Therefore, we leave this distribution unconstrained to accommodate a broader range of cognitive measures or transformed scores whose theoretical limit of performance may be negative.

The person-specific changes in peak performance, ∆ (i) , follow a normal distribution because they may take positive values (i.e., longer RTs) or negative values (i.e., shorter RTs) in our example: where β ∆ and σ ∆ denote the regression coefficient vector and standard deviation, respectively.

All three remaining parameters, namely between-burst forgetting (ϕ (i) ) , within-burst learning rates (r W (i) ), and intra-individual standard deviations (τ (i) ) are constrained to be positive, and follow similar lognormal distributions in 'logStan': where β ln(ϕ) , β ln(r) W , and β ln(τ ) denote the corresponding regression coefficient vectors, and σ ln(ϕ) , σ ln(r) W , and σ ln(τ ) denote the corresponding population-level standard deviations.

In the 'boundedStan' model, they simply follow bounded normal distributions (e.g.,

Priors for Population-Level Parameters

The above regression coefficients and standard deviation parameters are hyperparameters for which prior distributions must be specified. We set weakly informative priors on these hyperparameters to restrict estimation to plausible values while assigning low probabilities to unrealistic values (based on the theoretical scale of the data).

Specifically, we assign relatively diffuse priors (i.e., N (0, 100) for regression coefficients and N + (0, 100) for standard deviation parameters, with the normal distribution specified in terms of mean and variance).

Step-by-step Guidelines to Fitting the Bayesian Double Exponential Model in Stan

This section provides detailed guidance for fitting the multilevel model in Stan.

Replicable scripts can be found on our OSF page. 2 We will focus on the 'logStan' specification initially, and later show how we can achieve 'boundedStan' with minimal modifications of the presented code.

In the following scripts, we assume all required data are available, including: • nrPersons: number of participants; • N: total number of observations; • pInd: person index, which takes on values from 0 to nrPersons-1 in PyMC, and 1 to nrPersons in Stan/JAGS; • dayInd: measurement time in the study, corresponding to M (t,i) ; • dayInBurstInd: measurement time within the burst, corresponding to T (t,i) ; • burstTime: burst start time, corresponding to B (t,i) ; • notBurstOneInd: indicator for observations after the first burst, corresponding to I{Bn (t,i) > 1}; • RT: reaction time, corresponding to RT (t,i) ; • nrAssess: number of assessments per day, corresponding to A (t,i) ; • X: predictor matrix with nrPersons rows and nrCov columns

Step 0: Setting up R for analysis with Stan.

Load rstan, parallel, and coda. The parallel package supports parallel execution (i.e., each of the MCMC chains runs on its own core at the same time), and coda provides tools for handling posterior samples. Stan also requires a compilation phase. By setting auto_write = TRUE, R saves a compiled version of the model to the user's hard drive so that if the user runs the script again without changing the model, R will skip compilation and start sampling immediately. Furthermore, mc.cores specifies how many cores to use simultaneously, with parallel::detectCores() automatically detecting how many cores are available.

1 # Load packages 2 library ( rstan ) 3 library ( parallel ) 4 library ( coda ) 5 6 # Set up parallel computing in Stan 7 rstan _ options ( auto _ write = TRUE ) 8 options ( mc . cores = parallel :: detectCores () ) Step 1: Defining the "data" block.

Because Stan compiles to C++, users must declare each variable's type and dimensions (e.g., int for integers). In particular, pInd is declared as an array of integers because it serves as an index in the likelihood defined later, and indices must be integers.

The dimensions of the data are declared in square brackets. For instance, the time indicators (dayInd, dayInBurstInd, burstTime, notBurstOneInd), person indicator (pInd), and observed data (RT, nrAssess) are all of length N given that there are N total observations. Similarly, the predictor matrix has nrPersons rows and nrCov columns.

It is also useful to specify the valid ranges of variables (see, e.g., <lower=1> to indicate that values are always at least 1). The box below shows all declarations needed for a multiburst dataset for BDEM analysis. 9 data { 10 int < lower =1 > nrPersons ; // total number of persons int < lower =1 > N ; // total number of datapoints int pInd [ N ]; // which person 13 vector [ N ] dayInd ; // day nested in the study vector [ N ] dayInBurstInd ; // day within the burst vector [ N ] burstTime ; // burst start time in years vector [ N ] notBurstOneInd ; // is it the first burst vector [ N ] RT ; // all RT data vector [ N ] nrAssess ; // how many assessments that day int < lower =1 > nrCov ; // total number of predictors 20 matrix [ nrPersons , nrCov ] X ; // person predictor matrix 21 } Step 2: Defining the "parameters" block.

Model parameters, including both population-level and person-specific parameters, need similar declarations in the "parameters" block. The declarations below show that each person-specific parameter is stored in a vector of length nrPersons and that each vector of regression coefficients has length nrCov, the number of covariates supplied as data. Also, the range of the standard deviation parameters is limited to the positive real line (real<lower=0>). In some applications, like the one in our empirical illustration, it might also make sense to limit the range of the learning rate parameter, which would also be done in the below block (see example later).

First, we assign priors for population-level parameters, including both regression coefficients and standard deviation parameters. The next three boxes show consecutive fragments of a single model {} block in Stan (opened in the first listing and closed after the likelihood).

model { // Hyper -priors for regression coefficients betaLogrW ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaLogrC ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaLogPhi ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaLogSdE ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaLoggC ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaA ~normal (0 , 10) ; betaDelta ~normal (0 , 10) ; // Hyper -priors for standard deviation parameters logrWSd ~normal (0 , 10) ; logrCSd ~normal (0 , 10) ; logPhiSd ~normal (0 , 10) ; logSdESd ~normal (0 , 10) ; loggCSd ~normal (0 , 10) ; aSd ~normal (0 , 10) ; deltaSd ~normal (0 , 10) ;

Then we specify distributions for person-specific parameters as follows. The population means of the person-specific parameters are expressed as products of person-level predictors (X) and regression coefficients (e.g., betaA), except for g C(i) . In Stan, "*" denotes matrix-vector multiplication here.

// Population distributions ( i . e . , priors ) for person -specific // parameters logrW ~normal ( X * betaLogrW , logrWSd ) ; logrC ~normal ( X * betaLogrC , logrCSd ) ; logphi ~normal ( X * betaLogPhi , logPhiSd ) ; logsdE ~normal ( X * betaLogSdE , logSdESd ) ; loggC ~normal ( betaLoggC , loggCSd ) ; a ~normal ( X * betaA , aSd ) ; delta ~normal ( X * betaDelta , deltaSd ) ;

Then the likelihood is defined as follows. Stan also allows for vectorized formulations, so no for loops are needed when specifying the likelihood. Stan uses ".*" for element-wise multiplication. Notice that the model block will end after this part. // Likelihood ( see Equation 1) vector [ N ] mu_RT ; vector [ N ] sd_RT ; mu_RT = gC [ pInd ].* exp ( -rC [ pInd ].* dayInd ) + a [ pInd ] + delta [ pInd ].* burstTime + notBurstOneInd .*( phi [ pInd ] -delta [ pInd ]) .* exp ( -rW [ pInd ].* dayInBurstInd ) ; sd_RT = sdE [ pInd ]./ sqrt ( nrAssess ) ; RT ~normal ( mu_RT , sd_RT ) ; } // Close model block Step 4 (Optional): Defining the "generated quantities" block. The optional generated quantities block is placed after the model block. It computes additional quantities from each posterior draw without changing the posterior distribution being sampled. Here, we generate a replicated reaction time for each observation, stored in RT_pred, for use in posterior predictive checks. For each observation, normal_rng() draws a value from the normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as the likelihood in Step 3. After sampling, the replicated data can be compared with the observed RT values to assess how well the model reproduces features of the data. generated quantities { vector [ N ] RT_pred ; for ( n in 1: N ) { RT_pred [ n ] = normal_rng ( a [ pInd [ n ]] + delta [ pInd [ n ]] * burstTime [ n ] + gC [ pInd [ n ]] * exp ( -rC [ pInd [ n ]] * dayInd [ n ]) + notBurstOneInd [ n ] * ( phi [ pInd [ n ]] -delta [ pInd [ n ]]) * exp ( -rW [ pInd [ n ]] * dayInBurstInd [ n ]) , sdE [ pInd [ n ]] / sqrt ( nrAssess [ n ]) ) ; } } Step 5: Running the analysis and extracting the results.

With all blocks in the model script defined, we make it a string object, modelString, and save it in the BDEM.stan file. We then pass this model file, together with data (a list object), names of parameters of interest (see parameters), and initial values (see myinitsList) to the stan() function. For the MCMC settings, we specify 4 chains and 11,000 total iterations per chain, including 10,000 retained iterations and 1,000 warmup iterations (during warmup, Stan adapts its sampling algorithm; draws from this phase are not included in the final posterior sample.) Additionally, adapt_delta specifies the target acceptance probability during adaptation for the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS; Hoffman & Gelman, 2014). Setting it to a high value (0.99) generally produces smaller adapted step sizes, which may increase computation time but reduce divergent transitions. Another keyword, max_treedepth, is used to control the depth of the trees that the sampler evaluates during each iteration. Reaching the maximum allowed tree depth indicates that a sampling trajectory was terminated at the configured limit to avoid excessively long execution times. parameters <-c ( " rW " , " rC " , " phi " , " sdE " , " gC " , " a " , " delta " , " RT _ pred " , " betaLogrW " , " logrWSd " , " betaLogrC " , " logrCSd " , " betaLogPhi " , " logPhiSd " , " betaLogSdE " , " logSdESd " , " betaLoggC " , " loggCSd " , " betaA " , " aSd " , " betaDelta " ," deltaSd " In the alternative Stan parametrization, we keep the data block (Step 1) the same as before, but we change the declarations in Step 2. Comparing the 'logStan' and 'boundedStan' model specifications

While the 'logStan' parametrization follows the common statistical approach of modeling non-negative variables on the log scale, its regression coefficients must be back-transformed to interpret nonlinear effects on the original scale. Although this tutorial focuses on this parametrization, we also show that Stan provides a more straightforward way to constrain parameter values through range declarations. Regression coefficients from fitting 'boundedStan' do not need to be back-transformed, and correspond directly to linear effects. We compared these two approaches in a simulation study and found that they yielded comparable results in terms of person-specific parameter estimates and regression coefficients. One exception is that, using 'boundedStan', the recovery of population-level standard deviation was suboptimal (see below). For this reason, we generally do not recommend making inferences about the magnitude of between-person variances in learning rates from the 'boundedStan' approach.

However, we expect that practitioners are often interested primarily in the person-specific parameter estimates, and less so in estimating population-level variances. In such a scenario, there is a trade-off that users may choose to make: While the 'logStan' implementation may offer superior recovery of some of the structural parameters, compared to 'boundedStan' it comes with additional burdens in user-friendliness and interpretability.

We believe it is reasonable for practitioners to make a trade-off and choose 'boundedStan' for ease of use at the expense of calibration of the population variance parameters.

Estimation performance of the two approaches was compared via Monte Carlo simulation, the detailed results of which are reported in the Appendix, with a short summary provided here. In all the simulation studies, data were generated from the likelihood introduced in Equation ( 1), and positivity-constrained BDEM parameters were generated from lognormal population distributions, matching the 'logStan' parametrization. The two Stan implementations showed virtually indistinguishable performance on most parameters in terms of relative biases, root mean square errors, sensitivity, and coverage rates (see definitions of these metrics in the Appendix), except for the population-level parameters (e.g., coefficients and standard deviations) of the learning rate parameters, for which "boundedStan" yielded higher relative biases and lower coverage rates than "logStan" did. With both methods, the learning-rate parameters show much remaining uncertainty (i.e., high posterior variability), indicating that these parameters are generally difficult to learn from the limited within-person data we had. Specifically, for individual-specific learning rates, while relative biases were less than 0.1, the RMSEs were approximately one population standard deviation. Users should therefore be cautious when making individual-level inferences about learning-rate parameters with the data sizes tested in the simulations (i.e., 14 within-person observations per burst across 3 bursts).

Empirical Illustration

We illustrate the findings BDEM can yield by fitting it to high-frequency cognitive assessment data from the Effects of Stress on Cognitive Aging, Physiology, and Emotion (ESCAPE) study (Scott et al., 2015). Corresponding scripts and data can be found on this OSF page.

This measurement burst study explored associations between rumination, cognition, stress, and cognitive aging. Participants, aged 25 to 65, were drawn by systematic probability sampling from New York City registered-voter lists in the Bronx. Participants completed a maximum of four measurement bursts, about nine months apart. At each wave, bursts lasted for 14 days with ecological momentary assessments delivered on study smartphones five times a day. We will focus on analyzing data from the symbol search task (Sliwinski et al., 2018), in which each trial showed three symbol pairs across the top of the screen and two pairs at the bottom, and the participant had to choose, as quickly as possible, which of the two bottom pairs appeared among the three at the top. At each EMA, participants completed 12 trials, which we summarized as the median response time of the correct trials. For each day, we aggregated these medians into a daily mean response time score, which was modeled with BDEM.

Since this tutorial uses the ESCAPE data for methods demonstration purposes, we analyzed a subset of the data: only participants who were between 40 and 65 years of age at baseline. We also added noise to our selected set of covariates by grouping age into five-year intervals (e.g., ages 40-44 were coded as 40) and adding normally distributed noise with mean 0 and SD 0.5 to years of education. These values were then standardized and entered into the model as continuous predictors. Additionally, we removed RT outliers exceeding 3 SD from person's median and required at least 5 sessions per burst, which removed 1.4% of the original data points.

Sample characteristics, as shown in

Table 2, were as follows. We had 182 participants, of whom 52 (28.57%) completed one burst, 34 (18.68%) completed two bursts, 48 (26.37%) completed three bursts, and 48 (26.37%) completed four bursts. The mean age at baseline was 52.63 (SD = 6.76) years and 65.4% were female. The sample was racially and ethnically diverse with 82.97% identifying as non-White and 26.92% as Hispanic. The mean years of education was 15.41 (SD = 2.32) years. For this empirical analysis, we introduced a constraint to increase computational stability. This was the only deviation from the step-by-step procedure described above.

Specifically, we constrained the within-burst learning rate to lie between 0 and e1 ≈ 2.718 (declared on the log scale as: vector<upper=1>[nrPersons] logrW;). This parameter controls the slope of the negative exponentials from the second burst on. As can be seen in Figure 2, learning rates higher than 3 (i.e., very steep slopes = fast learning) are practically indistinguishable, as they reach the asymptote after 1 practice session (and this is already very extreme). Figure 2 illustrates this behavior at three slope-height (gain) settings, with learning speeds color-coded in each plot. This is a liberal constraint as we expect most learning rates to stay below 1, but it helps with computational efficiency. Such a constraint is not necessarily needed in every empirical application, but the current dataset was rather noisy (e.g., large within-person standard deviations around the learning slopes).

Sampling quality and fit

We ran four MCMC chains for 4,000 iterations each, discarding the first 1,000 iterations per chain as warmup. The minimum ESS was 404. ESS was > 3,000 for approximately 87% of parameters, and R < 1.05 for all parameters.

We calculated the R² statistic using posterior estimates of the individual-level parameters to assess model fit, and found it to be acceptable (.80). The R² measures how much of the observed variation in daily mean reaction times is accounted for by the model. density plots in Figure 4. For the Q-Q plot, posterior predictive draws of RT_pred in each MCMC iteration form a replicated data set from which we calculate quantiles. With K iterations, there are K values for each quantile; the plotted point is their mean and the error bar is their 95% interval. For well fitting models, these quantiles should line up around the diagonal, with 95% intervals covering it. For the density plot, we overlay the smoothed density of the observed data (thicker black line) with densities of replicated data sets (thinner blue lines) from the posterior predictive distribution. Overlap indicates that the model reproduces the overall distribution of reaction times. Both checks showed satisfactory model fit: observed and simulated quantiles line up well on the diagonal, and replicated density curves cover the observed curve closely.

Corresponding scripts and plots are available on the OSF directory.

Population-level Results

Population-level estimates for the seven cognitive markers are shown in Table 3 as posterior means and 95% posterior credible intervals (PCI). In the Bayesian framework, a 95% PCI is the range within which the parameter lies with 95% probability, and so describes uncertainty in the estimate. For each cognitive marker the table shows both the population mean (conditional on all predictors being zero, that is for women of average age and education) and the population standard deviation (SD), which the residual SD quantifying remaining individual differences. These values are shown on the original (back-transformed) scale of the parameters. Our tutorial code automatically returns this table after running the analysis. The distribution of person-specific posterior mean estimates of the seven cognitive markers is shown in Figure 5. For all parameters except learning rates (for which the numbers show exponential rate of change), the x-axis corresponds to seconds.

On average, within-burst retest gain (that kicks in after the first burst) shrunk by a factor of e -0.30 with each day of testing. Half of the warm-up present at the start of a burst is then realized by day 2 or 3 (ln(2)/0.30 ≈ 2.3 days), and 95% of it in 10 days (-ln(0.05)/0.30 ≈ 10 days).

Across-burst retest gains followed a similar pattern, with half of the study-long retest gain realized after ln(2)/0.24 ≈ 2.9 days and 95% afterln(0.05)/0.24 ≈ 12.5 days. These values correspond to days in the first burst because time index M is cumulative across the study. Explaining individual differences in cognitive markers

Predictor effects were estimated in the same BDEM analysis (one-stage regression modeling). Age and years of education were standardized and sex was coded 0 for women and 1 for men. Peak performance and change in peak performance were modeled on their original scale; therefore, the regression coefficients captured additive differences.

Forgetting, the two learning rates, and within-person variability were modeled on the log scale; their coefficients in the table therefore are mean ratios, exp(kβ), relative to a reference of 1. For within-burst learning, those ratios include the upper-bound adjustment.

Table 4 shows the posterior mean estimates, 95% PCIs, and probability of direction measures for the estimated regression coefficients. The probability of direction (p d ) is defined as the proportion of the posterior distribution that lies on the same side of the null value-0 for additive coefficients and 1 for mean ratios-as the posterior median (Makowski, Ben-Shachar, Chen, & Lüdecke, 2019). In the present study, inference was based on the p d , and effects with p d between 90% and 95% were described as possibly credible, and those above 95% as credible effects.

Here we highlight the credible effects. Age and peak performance on the symbol search task were credibly associated: a 1 SD increase in age predicted a 0.10 s slower peak reaction time (95% PCI [0.00, 0.20], p d = 0.97). Relative to the population-level SD of peak performance (0.56 s), this is a small effect (0.10/0.56 = 0.18). Age was also associated with forgetting between bursts (M = 1.26, 95% PCI [0.98, 1.62], p d = 0.96), or about 26% more forgetting for a 1 SD increase in age. The same age difference was associated with a 20% decrease in the across-burst learning rate (M = 0.80, [0.61, 1.04], p d = 0.95).

There were also sex differences in across-burst learning rates: for male participants, the mean across-burst learning rate was around 49% lower than for women (M = 0.51, [0.27, 0.90], p d = 0.98). Interestingly, people with more years of education took more practice days to reach their asymptote (slower within-burst learning rate, M = 0.71, [0.42, 1.06]; p d = 0.95). Finally, performance inconsistency decreased with years of education (lower within-person variability, M = 0.94, [0.88, 1.00]; p d = 0.96). of Education 0.94 0.88 1.00 0.96

Discussion

Interest in intensive, mobile, and ecological cognitive assessment continues to grow, but retest effects can easily masquerade as change when the same tasks are repeated at high frequency. At the same time, hierarchical Bayesian modeling has become a realistic default in many fields, with mature, well-documented engines such as Stan, PyMC, and JAGS. We believe our hands-on tutorial, connecting a purpose-built retest model to these tools, is therefore timely: It helps researchers separate substantive dynamics from measurement-driven improvement in designs that are increasingly common but statistically easy to misinterpret.

We demonstrated how to fit the BDEM in Stan to disentangle retest effects from longitudinal cognitive change in measurement burst designs. The BDEM can also quantify individual differences in seven different cognitive markers and regress these markers on covariates in a one-step estimation. Simulation studies with Stan, PyMC, and JAGS (see Supplementary Materials) showed that while all three approaches provided reliable parameter recovery, they presented distinct trade-offs in modeling flexibility, sampling efficiency, and computational time.

Our empirical example showed that capturing individual differences in retest learning effects (rather than just separating them out) can provide a richer picture of cognitive functioning. The model identified several credible predictor effects on the dynamics of retest learning and forgetting, such as older adults showing more forgetting between bursts, and slower across burst learning rates.

Simulation results indicated that most model parameters, including person-specific parameters, were well recovered in both Stan model formulations and in the other Bayesian software engines (i.e., PyMC and JAGS). The most challenging cognitive marker to estimate was the within-burst learning rate, which exhibited larger biases than the other parameters, low sensitivity in very small samples and greater discrepancy between the different model formulations across the three software programs. More details on implementation constraints and results from simulation studies comparing Stan, JAGS and PyMC can be found in the Supplementary Materials.

One limitation of the current approach is the conditionally Gaussian likelihood, which may be a poor fit for the right-skewed distribution of RTs. An extension of the BDEM to accommodate skewed likelihood families would be a valuable direction for future research.

However, in EMA studies, raw RT data are rarely used, instead aggregates are calculated by typically averaging 50-100 trials per day per individual (e.g., from up to 5 sessions per day with 10-20 trials in each session, see e.g., Moore, Swendsen, and Depp (2017)). These aggregates don't exhibit the same skewness, which could be checked with our recommended posterior predictive checks.

The code examples provided in the present article can be readily extended in different ways to accommodate different applications. For example, one can add predictors to explain individual differences in the across-study gain parameter if needed, following the same logic used for the forgetting parameter. We could also allow for time-varying cognitive features to accommodate more complex real-world assumptions. While the current model only allows for peak performance to change from burst to burst, modeling changes in learning rate or forgetting across bursts would allow researchers to test whether changes in these markers across the years could be potential indicators of subtle cognitive decline. Finally, although lower scores were better in the current example, the model can accommodate the bounded growth shape shown in Figure 6 by placing a negative sign before both the gain parameter and the expression (ϕ (i) -∆ (i) ) in line 3 of Equation ( 1). The SDs of these markers in Table 3 are calculated using Equation (3).

Simulation Study 1: Comparisons Between boundedStan and logStan

This study aims to evaluate and compare the performance of two Stan models by fitting them to the simulated data described below. Parameters are back-transformed to their original scale to facilitate a direction comparison.

Data Generation

Data are simulated based on the model specified in Equation 1. The true values for population-level parameters were set based on estimation results from previous empirical studies (Oravecz, Sliwinski, et al., 2025; Oravecz, Vandekerckhove, et al., 2025) (see tables below for a full list of true values). In general, we simulated data with medium effect sizes.

For instance, for the dummy predictor of the person-specific parameter θ, the regression coefficient was set such that the mean difference between the two groups divided by the standard deviation of θ (i.e., ) was close to 0.5; similarly, for the continuous predictor, we set the marginal effect of the predictor divided by the standard deviation of θ (i.e., ) close to 0.5 (see equations below).

In terms of sample size, we considered two conditions, P = 100 and P = 200. Under both conditions, each person was simulated to have 3 bursts of data, 14 days per burst, such that each person had 14 ×3 = 42 data points. For both conditions, 500 datasets were generated. The data generation code can be found on the OSF page.

Parameter Transformations Between logStan and boundedStan

The transformations described below are based on the model without upper bounds, which will be used in this simulation study. The equations need to be adjusted if there are upper bounds added.

boundedStan.

The "boundedStan" model utilizes a normal distribution constrained at [0, ∞) such that E[θ i ] = µ i and V ar(θ i ) = σ 2 , where µ i is defined as: where X 1,i is a dummy predictor and X 2,i is a standardized continuous predictor.

logStan.

The simulation generates data where the positive person-specific parameters follow a lognormal distribution such that ln(θ i ) ∼ N (µ l,i , σ 2 l ), where

The original-scale reference mean β0 and standard deviation σ are calculated using Equations ( 2) and (3), respectively, with X 1,i = X 2,i = 0.

Because the relationship between the predictors and the expected value is non-linear in the "logStan" model, the dummy slope and continuous slope are defined approximately as the marginal effects at the reference group mean (where X 1,i = 0 and X 2,i = 0).

Similarly, the population-level standard deviation is also evaluated at the origin (where X 1,i = 0 and X 2,i = 0). While these definitions do not represent the "exact" target parameters in the "boundedStan" model, they provide the best approximation and allow for a direct comparison between the two models on the original scale.

Performance Measures

The following summary statistics were calculated to help evaluate the estimation and sampling performance.

Suppose that H Monte Carlo (MC) replications are implemented in a simulation, θ is the true value of a particular parameter, and the point and standard error estimates of θ in the hth (h = 1, . . . , H) replication are θh and SE θh , respectively. Let the average of point estimates across H replications be θ, then the relative bias, standard error (SE), empirical standard error (ESE) and root mean square error (RMSE) are defined as follows:

The ESE diagnostic in Equation ( 17) is the standard deviation of the point estimates across MC replications (Morris, White, & Crowther, 2019), that can be compared with the average model-based SE in Equation ( 16) to indicate whether the posterior standard deviations are well calibrated.

Among these measures, a relative bias (which applies only to non-zero true values) smaller than 0.1 indicates relatively good estimation performance, while other measures are subject to the scale of the true parameter value. In addition, we also considered (1) sensitivity (similar to power in the frequentist framework), defined as the proportion of replications whose credible intervals do not contain 0. A sensitivity value close to 1 indicates a high level of sensitivity to the effect size (i.e., high power in detecting the effect size if conceptually understood in the frequentist framework); (2) coverage rates, defined as the percentages of replications whose credible intervals contain the true values. A coverage rate close to the nominal rate of 95% would be considered ideal.

Sampling Diagnostics

The sampling quality and convergence problems were evaluated by two diagnostic statistics (Gelman et al., 2013): (1) the effective sample size (ESS), which describes how many posterior draws in the MCMC procedure can be regarded as independent. We also report ESS per second, calculated as the average ESS across all parameters divided by the total runtime, which captures the trade-off between computational time and sampling quality; and (2) R, which describes the ratio of the overall variance of posterior samples across chains to the within-chain variance, and is indicative of convergence issues. For this learning-rate effect and -0.15 for the continuous across-burst learning-rate effect, whereas logStan's regression coefficients all had absolute relative biases below 0.10. Coefficient RMSEs and coverage nevertheless remained broadly comparable. Most population SDs were also recovered well by logStan, while boundedStan underestimated the two learning-rate SDs by approximately 23%, with coverage of 86% for σ r W and 72% for σ r C.

Increasing the sample size to P = 200 generally reduced coefficient RMSEs and improved sensitivity in both parameterizations. Sensitivity exceeded 0.80 for all continuous effects and for binary effects outside the learning-rate features, while coefficient coverage generally remained around 95%. The continuous within-burst learning-rate effect showed a particularly clear improvement in sensitivity, rising from approximately 0.50 to above 0.80.

Binary learning-rate effects also became easier to detect, although their sensitivity remained lower (0.32-0.59). The remaining differences were largely unchanged: boundedStan's relative bias for the continuous within-burst effect decreased in magnitude to -0.15, but that for the continuous across-burst effect increased in magnitude to -0.18, with coverage of 83%.

Bias in its learning-rate SDs persisted, and coverage fell to 74% and 40%, respectively, compared with approximately nominal coverage in logStan. Thus, a larger sample improved precision and detection for most effects, while logStan retained an advantage for several population-level learning-rate quantities. The suboptimal performance of boundedStan on learning rate parameters was likely due to the mismatch between the constrained idiom and the log-normal data-generating process rather than to any deficiency of the engines themselves.

Person-Specific Parameters. At P = 100, both models showed small absolute relative biases (at or below 0.10) and coverage around 95% for most person-specific markers. RMSEs were below 0.10 for asymptotic performance, its change, and intra-individual variability. Although the biases for learning rates remained small, the RMSEs were substantial relative to the reference population SD. Recovery was similar across parameterizations, with slightly lower learning-rate coverage in boundedStan (91% versus 94% in logStan).

At P = 200, person-specific biases, RMSEs, and coverage changed little in either model, and the small coverage difference for learning rates persisted. Person-specific recovery was therefore broadly comparable across models, while the limited improvement with more participants indicates that individual learning-rates are weakly identifiable and their estimates require caution with data sizes tested in the simulations (i.e., within-person 14 data points per per burst, 3 bursts).

Appendix Population-Level Means, Standard Deviations, and Predictor Effects

For cognitive markers modeled on the log scale, we derive population-level means, standard deviations, and predictor effects on the original scale, with and without an upper bound. Table 4 expresses predictor effects as ratios of conditional population means. Let θ i denote such a marker, with ln(θ i ) ∼ N (µ l,i , σ 2 l ) and µ l,i = β l,0 + j β l,j X j,i . For predictor j, we compare X j,i = 1 with X j,i = 0, setting all other predictors to zero in both profiles. We write X -j,i = 0 for this setting of the other predictors, so the two log-scale locations are β l,0 + β l,j and β l,0 , respectively. This one-unit increase corresponds to a one-standard-deviation increase for standardized age or education, or a change from women (0) to men (1) for sex. A ratio of 1 indicates no change in the conditional mean; ratios above or below 1 indicate a larger or smaller mean, respectively. For example, a ratio of 1.26 represents a 26% larger mean, whereas a ratio of 0.80 represents a 20% smaller mean.

Peak performance and change in peak performance retain their additive coefficient interpretation and are not transformed into ratios.

Results

Computational Time. The computational time was calculated as the average execution time across all simulation replications. Results showed that the two Stan models used similar amount of time -around 2,500 seconds under P =100 and 5,000 seconds under P =200.

Sampling Diagnostics.

Based on our selection criteria (i.e., all parameters had R < 1.1 and at least 95% of them had ESS > 400), we kept 99-100% and 98-99% of replications for logStan and boundedStan, respectively. In terms of ESS per second, under P =100, logStan showed better mixing relative to the runtime (22/s) than boundedStan (14/s), while under P = 200, the two models yielded similar results (10/s).

Performance Measures. This subsection compares relative bias, RMSE, sensitivity, and coverage for boundedStan and logStan on the original parameter scale.

Figures 7-10 summarize recovery, and Tables 6, 5, 8, and 7 provide the full results.

Population-level Parameters. At P = 100, both parameterizations recovered most regression coefficients well, with absolute relative biases below 0.10, RMSEs below 0.10, and coverage around 95%. Their performance was particularly similar for asymptotic performance, its change, forgetting, and intra-individual variability. Sensitivity was generally higher for continuous than binary predictors, with the learning-rate effects being the most difficult to detect: sensitivity for the binary learning-rate effects was 0.23-0.38 in both models.

The model captures multiple trends at once, including within-burst retest learning (each exponential curve declines), forgetting (each new curve starts higher than the previous one ended), across-burst retest learning (worse performance in the beginning of the study than at the end), and across-burst change in peak performance (the asymptote of each exponential curve is higher than the last).
